fourierTransform.title: Fourier transform: pulse and sinc
fourierTransform.subtitle: A narrower pulse gives a wider main lobe; the pulse area sets the DC value. Drag the width and watch time and frequency trade places.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: x(t) is a rectangle of width τ and height A, centred at the origin.

plot.timeDescription: The shaded area is Aτ, which is also X(0).
plot.spectrumDescription: The dashed line marks the first zero. Side lobes decay as frequency grows.

insight.title: What to notice
insight.duality: Rectangle ↔ sinc is a fundamental pair: the boxier the time signal, the more spread-out the spectrum.
insight.scaling: Halve τ and the main lobe doubles in width; double A and the whole spectrum doubles in height.
insight.zeros: Zeros sit at f = k/τ (k = ±1, ±2, ...), not at arbitrary frequencies.
insight.uncertainty: A narrow time signal needs a wide band. This is the signals version of an uncertainty principle.

experiment.predict: Compute 1/τ first, then check the first zero on the plot.
experiment.connect: Fix τ and change only A: the zeros stay put while the height scales.

laplace.title: Laplace transform: poles and the ROC
laplace.subtitle: Drag a conjugate pole pair across the imaginary axis: left half-plane decays, the axis oscillates, the right half-plane grows. The ROC decides causality and stability.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: The poles are at σ ± jω. This lab assumes a causal system, so the ROC lies to the right of the rightmost pole.
controls.sigmaHint: σ < 0 is stable, σ = 0 is marginal, σ > 0 is unstable.
controls.omegaHint: ω sets the oscillation rate; |σ| sets how fast the envelope decays or grows.

readouts.stabilityHint: Check whether every pole is in the left half-plane
readouts.decayTitle: Read the response from the poles
readouts.decayDescription: The real part controls the envelope and the imaginary part controls oscillation; together they determine h(t).
readouts.excludesAxis: Does not include the jω axis

plot.pzDescription: The shaded region is to the right of the rightmost pole; a causal ROC extends to the right.
plot.impulseDescription: The envelope is e^{σt}; ω controls the oscillation.
plot.clipped: Peak is about {peak}; the vertical axis is clipped.

insight.title: What to notice
insight.left: A left half-plane pole gives an e^{σt} decaying envelope: stable.
insight.axis: A simple pole on the imaginary axis gives constant oscillation: marginal.
insight.right: A right half-plane pole gives a growing envelope: unstable.
insight.roc: The ROC contains the jω axis if and only if the system is stable. For a causal system the ROC is to the right of the rightmost pole.

experiment.title: Try this
experiment.cross: Move σ from −2 to 1 slowly. Predict how the envelope of h(t) changes.
experiment.omega: Fix σ and change only ω: the oscillation gets denser while the envelope stays the same.
experiment.roc: At σ = 0, does the ROC still contain the jω axis? Is the system stable?

secondOrder.title: Second-order systems: damping decides
secondOrder.subtitle: ζ controls overshoot and ωn controls speed. Move from underdamped to overdamped and watch peak time and settling time.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: ζ is the damping ratio and ωn is the undamped natural frequency. The step response settles at 1.
controls.zetaHint: ζ < 1 is underdamped, ζ = 1 is critical, ζ > 1 is overdamped.
controls.naturalFrequencyHint: A larger ωn makes the whole response faster.

plot.title: Step response
plot.description: The dashed line is the final value 1; the marker is the first peak.

insight.title: What to notice
insight.under: A smaller ζ means more overshoot and ringing, but a faster rise.
insight.critical: At ζ = 1 there is no overshoot: the fastest response without overshoot.
insight.over: For ζ > 1 there is no overshoot, but the two real poles separate and the response slows down.
insight.natural: Fix ζ and increase ωn: the whole response is compressed in time.

experiment.title: Try this
experiment.fixed: Fix ωn = 2 and move ζ from 0.1 to 1.0, recording the overshoot.
experiment.cross: Set ζ exactly to 1 and confirm that the overshoot is zero.
experiment.compare: Compare the settling time at ζ = 0.5 and ζ = 2, and explain why overdamped is not always faster.

modulation.title: Modulation: moving the spectrum to a carrier
modulation.subtitle: Use a baseband cosine to control the carrier amplitude. Inspect the carrier, the sidebands, and the overmodulation that appears when m > 1.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: fm is the baseband frequency, fc is the carrier and m is the modulation index.
controls.indexHint: When m > 1 the envelope crosses zero: overmodulation.

readouts.overmodulatedHint: The envelope inverts and envelope detection distorts

plot.timeDescription: The dashed curves are ±[1 + m cos(2πfm t)], which set the envelope of the modulated signal.
plot.spectrumDescription: Modulation moves the baseband spectrum to either side of fc; each line height depends on m.

insight.title: What to notice
insight.shift: Multiplication moves the baseband spectrum to ±fc; it is a shift, not a copy.
insight.sidebands: Single-tone modulation produces only two sidebands, at fc − fm and fc + fm.
insight.bandwidth: AM bandwidth is twice the baseband bandwidth: B = 2fm.
insight.overmodulation: When m > 1 the envelope goes negative, so simple envelope detection cannot recover the baseband.

experiment.title: Try this
experiment.zero: Set m = 0 and watch the sidebands disappear, leaving only the carrier.
experiment.increase: Move m from 0.5 to 1.4 and compare the envelope with the spectral lines.
experiment.observe: Fix m and change fc: the sideband spacing depends only on fm.

energy-signal-power.thought: You may be equating infinite duration with a power signal.
energy-signal-power.correction: Infinite duration does not imply nonzero average power. Check whether the squared integral converges.

energy-signal-neither.thought: You may think infinite duration always makes total energy diverge.
energy-signal-neither.correction: Exponential decay can make an improper integral converge. Square the signal before integrating.

energy-signal-both.thought: You may think finite energy also means finite nonzero average power.
energy-signal-both.correction: Finite energy divided by an unbounded observation interval tends to zero power. The two definitions do not overlap.

convolution-shift-direction.thought: You may be interpreting δ(t−2) as a left shift.
convolution-shift-direction.correction: Set its argument to zero: the impulse is at t=2. A delayed impulse delays the convolution output.

convolution-shift-scale.thought: You may be confusing time shifting with time scaling.
convolution-shift-scale.correction: x(2t) changes duration. Convolution with a delayed impulse changes time position only.

convolution-shift-ignore.thought: You may remember the identity with δ(t) but have dropped the delay.
convolution-shift-ignore.correction: Retain the shift in the impulse argument when applying the sifting property.

step-response-half.thought: You may be treating exponential approach as linear growth.
step-response-half.correction: A time constant is not the half-rise time. Substitute t/τ=1 into the exponential.

step-response-two-tau.thought: You may be mixing up the response fractions at one and two time constants.
step-response-two-tau.correction: Compute the dimensionless ratio t/τ before choosing a memorized percentage.

step-response-settling.thought: You may be treating one time constant as an almost settled response.
step-response-settling.correction: Distinguish 1τ from 3τ and 5τ. The response approaches its final value asymptotically.

aliasing-no-fold.thought: You may have kept the original frequency without folding it into the first Nyquist interval.
aliasing-no-fold.correction: Check f0 against fs/2, then take the appropriate difference from an integer multiple of fs.

aliasing-sample-rate.thought: You may have confused the sampling rate with the apparent signal frequency.
aliasing-sample-rate.correction: fs sets the spacing of spectral replicas. The apparent frequency comes from their folded position.

aliasing-add-frequencies.thought: You may have used a replica location as the baseband frequency.
aliasing-add-frequencies.correction: f0+fs is one replica location. Fold it back into [0, fs/2].

nyquist-equal.thought: You may think one sample per cycle is sufficient for reconstruction.
nyquist-equal.correction: The Nyquist rate is twice the highest frequency. Practical sampling also needs margin.

nyquist-half.thought: You may have inverted the relationship between sample rate and highest frequency.
nyquist-half.correction: Write the relationship between fs and 2fmax. A lower sample rate increases aliasing risk.

nyquist-double-again.thought: You may have applied the factor of two twice.
nyquist-double-again.correction: The question asks for the theoretical Nyquist rate. Engineering margin does not change its definition.

square-wave-even.thought: You may be confusing even symmetry with half-wave symmetry.
square-wave-even.correction: Even symmetry removes sine terms. Vanishing even harmonics requires the appropriate half-wave antisymmetry.

square-wave-period.thought: You may think periodicity alone eliminates even harmonics.
square-wave-period.correction: Periodicity gives discrete harmonics. Symmetry determines which coefficients vanish.

square-wave-energy.thought: You may be using energy classification to explain missing harmonics.
square-wave-energy.correction: A nonzero persistent periodic square wave is usually a power signal. Its symmetry determines vanishing coefficients.

pulse-spectrum-same-width.thought: You may think time width and frequency width change in the same direction.
pulse-spectrum-same-width.correction: Write the first spectral zero as 1/T before deciding how it moves.

pulse-spectrum-direct.thought: You may have focused on spectral height and missed the effect of width on the zeros.
pulse-spectrum-direct.correction: Spectral height and main-lobe width are different quantities. Zero spacing depends on pulse width.

pulse-spectrum-nonmonotonic.thought: You may be confusing sinc oscillations with a nonmonotonic change in main-lobe width.
pulse-spectrum-nonmonotonic.correction: Define the main lobe between its first zeros, then compare 1/T.

time-constant-inverse.thought: You may think a larger time constant means a faster response and wider bandwidth.
time-constant-inverse.correction: Use fc=1/(2πτ). A slower response has a narrower bandwidth.

time-constant-independent.thought: You may be treating time and frequency responses as independent.
time-constant-independent.correction: The same pole controls both. τ determines response speed and cutoff frequency.

time-constant-peaking.thought: You may be applying second-order resonance intuition to a first-order system.
time-constant-peaking.correction: For a fixed-gain first-order low-pass system, cutoff frequency is inversely proportional to τ.

damping-more-overshoot.thought: You may think stronger damping increases oscillation.
damping-more-overshoot.correction: Damping dissipates oscillatory energy. Check the overshoot formula within the underdamped range.

damping-no-effect.thought: You may have considered natural frequency while overlooking damping.
damping-no-effect.correction: Natural frequency and damping ratio play different roles. Changing ζ changes overshoot and decay.

damping-infinite.thought: You may be mistaking a finite change in positive damping for instability.
damping-infinite.correction: The standard systems with ζ=0.3 and ζ=0.7 are both stable. Compare their finite overshoot values.

rhp-stable.thought: You may have overlooked the growth caused by a positive pole real part.
rhp-stable.correction: A causal system with a right-half-plane pole has a growing response. Check whether its ROC contains the imaginary axis.

rhp-marginal.thought: You may be confusing right-half-plane poles with simple imaginary-axis poles.
rhp-marginal.correction: Positive real parts produce growth. Zero real parts can produce the sustained-oscillation boundary case.

rhp-undecidable.thought: You may know stability depends on the ROC but have missed the stated causality.
rhp-undecidable.correction: For a causal rational system, the ROC is right of the rightmost pole. A right-half-plane pole then excludes the imaginary axis.

am-single-sideband.thought: You may have counted only one sideband.
am-single-sideband.correction: For ordinary double-sideband AM, there is one sideband on each side of the carrier.

am-double-sideband-twice.thought: You may have counted both sidebands twice.
am-double-sideband-twice.correction: Subtract fc−fm from fc+fm directly, without applying another factor of two.

am-half.thought: You may have inverted the relationship between baseband frequency and bandwidth.
am-half.correction: Mark the outer sidebands first, then calculate their separation.

imaginary-axis-decay.thought: You may be treating a nonzero imaginary part as the source of decay.
imaginary-axis-decay.correction: The imaginary part controls oscillation. The real part controls the envelope and is zero on the imaginary axis.

imaginary-axis-real.thought: You may be treating imaginary conjugate poles as negative real poles.
imaginary-axis-real.correction: Negative real poles produce nonoscillatory decay. Imaginary conjugate poles produce sinusoidal terms.

imaginary-axis-grow.thought: You may be confusing nonzero oscillation frequency with envelope growth.
imaginary-axis-grow.correction: Check σ in e^(σt). On the imaginary axis σ=0, so the envelope does not grow.

nyquist.explain: The threshold is 8 kHz. Equality does not universally reconstruct components at the boundary; practical sampling also needs an antialias transition band.

square-wave.prompt: Why does an ideal zero-mean, 50%-duty bipolar square wave (±A) have no even harmonics?
square-wave.explain: Half-wave antisymmetry x(t+T/2)=−x(t) removes DC and even harmonics. Odd symmetry alone is not sufficient.

pulse-spectrum.prompt: As a rectangular pulse gets wider, its main spectral lobe becomes?
pulse-spectrum.explain: Widening in time compresses the spectrum: the main-lobe width scales with 1/τ.

time-constant.prompt: For the standard first-order low-pass H(s)=K/(1+τs), τ>0, how does increasing τ at fixed K affect the −3 dB cutoff?
time-constant.explain: ωc=1/τ and fc=1/(2πτ), so a larger τ lowers the cutoff.

damping.prompt: For H(s)=ωn²/(s²+2ζωns+ωn²), ωn>0, how does zero-state unit-step overshoot change as ζ rises from 0.3 to 0.7?
damping.explain: For 0<ζ<1, Mp=e^(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)) decreases as ζ increases. This uses the stated standard zero-free form.

right-half-plane.prompt: A causal continuous-time LTI system has a proper, reduced rational H(s) with a right-half-plane pole. Is it BIBO stable?
right-half-plane.explain: An uncancelled RHP pole produces a growing mode; the causal ROC excludes part of the imaginary axis, so the system is not BIBO stable.

am-bandwidth.prompt: For single-tone double-sideband AM with fc>fm>0, what is the bandwidth between its positive-frequency sidebands?
am-bandwidth.explain: The sidebands lie at fc−fm and fc+fm, giving bandwidth 2fm. This is not the SSB bandwidth.

imaginary-axis.prompt: A causal rational system has uncancelled simple poles at s=±jω0, ω0>0, with nonzero residues. How does their real impulse-response mode behave?
imaginary-axis.explain: This pole pair contributes a constant-amplitude sinusoid. This describes that component, not the entire response if other poles exist.

finite-energy-power.prompt: A nonzero signal has finite total energy E=3. What is its two-sided time-average power?
finite-energy-power.explain: P=lim(E_T/(2T))=0: energy is bounded while observation length tends to infinity.

cosine-average-power.prompt: What is the average power of x(t)=2cos(3t)?
cosine-average-power.explain: The period average of cos² is 1/2, so P=2²/2=2.

rectangle-energy.prompt: A rectangle has amplitude 2 on [0,3] seconds and is zero elsewhere. What is its energy?

exponential-energy.prompt: What is the energy of x(t)=2e^(−2t)u(t)?

angular-to-hertz.prompt: An angular frequency is ω=40π rad/s. What is its frequency in Hz?

harmonic-period.prompt: For x(t)=cos(2t)+cos(4t), its fundamental period is T=kπ seconds. What is k?
harmonic-period.explain: The frequencies are in a 1:2 ratio, so ω0=2 rad/s and T=2π/2.

time-width-scale.prompt: x(t) has support width 12 seconds. What is the support width of x(3t)?
time-width-scale.explain: Time compression by 3 divides width by 3: 4 seconds.

support-delay-scale.prompt: x(t) is supported on [0,2]. What is the left endpoint of the support of x(2t−4)?

energy-time-scale.prompt: The energy of x(t) is 12. What is the energy of x(-3t)?
energy-time-scale.explain: A change of variable gives Enew=Eold/|a|=4.

impulse-sifting.prompt: What is ∫(t²+3)δ(t−2)dt over the real line?
impulse-sifting.explain: Sifting evaluates the polynomial at t=2: 7.

linear-superposition.prompt: For y(t)=2x(t), at one instant x₁=3 and x₂=4. What is the output for x₁+x₂?
linear-superposition.explain: T(x₁+x₂)=2(3+4)=14, the sum of the separate outputs.

square-homogeneity.prompt: For the nonlinear system T[x]=x² and x=3 at one instant, what is T[2x]?

delay-causality.prompt: For y(t)=x(t−1) on real-line signals, which classification is correct?
delay-causality.explain: It uses past input, so it is causal but not memoryless.

advance-causality.explain: The output at t needs the future input at t+1.

time-varying-multiplier.prompt: Is y(t)=t^1x(t) time invariant on the real line?
time-varying-multiplier.option1: Yes: all multipliers are time invariant
time-varying-multiplier.option3: No: the explicit time coefficient fails the shift test
time-varying-multiplier.option4: The system is defined only for zero input
time-varying-multiplier.explain: Shifting the input gives t^n x(t−t0), while shifting the output gives (t−t0)^n x(t−t0); these generally differ.

bounded-gain.prompt: For y=3x and |x(t)|≤2, what is the tight uniform bound on |y(t)|?
bounded-gain.explain: |y|=3|x|≤6; a constant boundary input attains this bound.

rc-time-units.prompt: For RC y′+y=x, R=2 kΩ and C=100 μF. What is the time constant in seconds?

total-response.prompt: At one instant, a linear system has zero-input response 5 and zero-state response -2. What is its total response?
total-response.explain: The total response is their sum: 5+(-2)=3.

decay-exponent.prompt: For y′+2y=0 and y=Ce^(λt), what is λ?

constant-forced-response.prompt: For y′+2y=6, what is the stable constant steady-state value?
constant-forced-response.explain: At steady state y′=0, so y∞=6/2=3.

impulse-state-jump.prompt: For y′+2y=3δ(t) and y(0−)=1, what is y(0+)?
impulse-state-jump.explain: Integrating across zero gives Δy=3, hence y(0+)=4.

second-order-jump.prompt: For y″+3y′+2y=2δ(t), with finite y(0−) and y′(0−)=1, find y′(0+).
second-order-jump.explain: With no δ′ input, y is continuous; matching δ gives Δy′=2, so the result is 3.

zero-input-initial.prompt: For y′+2y=x and y(0−)=3, what is A in the zero-input response A e^(−2t), t≥0?
zero-input-initial.explain: Set the input to zero. With no impulse jump, A=y(0+)=3.

impulse-step-final.prompt: For h(t)=4e^(−2t)u(t), what is the final zero-state unit-step response?

step-impulse-coefficient.prompt: The zero-state step response is g(t)=2(1−e^(−3t))u(t). In h(t)=A e^(−3t)u(t), what is A?
step-impulse-coefficient.explain: h=g′. Since g is continuous and zero at the origin, there is no δ term; A=6.

impulse-convolution-gain.prompt: In x(t)*[2δ(t−3)]=A x(t−3), what is A?
impulse-convolution-gain.explain: The impulse delay shifts the signal and its weight remains the gain 2.

rectangle-convolution-peak.prompt: Two unit-amplitude causal rectangles have widths 2 s and 5 s. What is their convolution peak?
rectangle-convolution-peak.explain: The peak is the maximum overlap length min(2,5)=2.

rectangle-convolution-width.prompt: Two unit causal rectangles are supported on [0,2] and [0,3]. What is the width of the closure of their convolution support?

equal-exponential-convolution.prompt: x=2e^(−1t)u(t) and h=3e^(−1t)u(t). Their convolution is A t e^(−1t)u(t). Find A.
equal-exponential-convolution.explain: The exponential product is e^(−1t) and the integration interval has length t, giving A=6.

cascade-impulse-gain.prompt: Two cascaded LTI systems have h₁=2δ(t) and h₂=3δ(t). Find A in h=Aδ(t).
cascade-impulse-gain.explain: Cascade uses convolution; δ*δ=δ, so gains multiply to 6.

parallel-impulse-gain.prompt: Two parallel LTI branches share an input and their outputs add, with h₁=2δ(t), h₂=3δ(t). What is the total impulse weight?
parallel-impulse-gain.explain: Parallel impulse responses add, giving weight 5.

autocorrelation-zero.prompt: A real rectangle has amplitude 2 on [0,3]. With Rxx(τ)=∫x(t)x(t−τ)dt, find Rxx(0).

autocorrelation-overlap.prompt: x(t) is a unit rectangle on [0,4]. For Rxx(τ)=∫x(t)x(t−τ)dt, find Rxx(1).
autocorrelation-overlap.explain: The overlap length and correlation value are 4−1=3.

continuous-convolution-step.prompt: For a Riemann approximation of continuous convolution, discrete conv gives 120 at a sample and dt=0.01 s. What is the integral approximation?
continuous-convolution-step.explain: Multiply the discrete sum by the integration step: 120×0.01=1.2.

fourier-fundamental-frequency.prompt: For period T=0.02 s, what is the Fourier-series line spacing in Hz?

fourier-cosine-coefficient.prompt: For x(t)=2+4cos(Ωt), what is complex Fourier-series coefficient F₁?
fourier-cosine-coefficient.explain: The cosine splits into positive and negative frequencies, each with coefficient 2.

pulse-train-average.prompt: A periodic pulse train has high level 2, low level 0 and duty cycle 25%. What is its DC coefficient?
pulse-train-average.explain: The period average is amplitude × duty cycle=0.5.

fourier-scale-dc.prompt: An integrable signal has X(j0)=12. For y(t)=x(3t), find Y(j0).
fourier-scale-dc.explain: Time scaling gives Y(jω)=X(jω/3)/3, hence Y(j0)=4.

fourier-delay-phase.prompt: For y(t)=x(t−2), what unwrapped phase in rad does the delay factor add at ω=3 rad/s?
fourier-delay-phase.explain: The delay factor e^(−jωtd) adds phase −ωtd=-6 rad.

modulation-upper-edge.prompt: A baseband spectrum is supported on [−3,3] kHz and is multiplied by a 100 kHz cosine. What is the upper edge of the translated positive-frequency support?
modulation-upper-edge.explain: The spectrum shifts to ±fc; the upper edge is fc+B=103 kHz.

sinusoidal-output-amplitude.prompt: A stable LTI system has |H|=0.5 at the input cosine frequency and input amplitude 6. What is its sinusoidal steady-state output amplitude?
sinusoidal-output-amplitude.explain: The output amplitude is |H|A=3 at the same frequency.

linear-phase-delay.prompt: For H(jω)=2e^(−j3ω), what is the group delay in seconds?

parseval-energy.prompt: Under the angular-frequency Fourier convention, ∫|X(jω)|²dω=8π. What is the total energy?

rectangle-first-zero.prompt: A single unit rectangle has width 0.02 s. What is its first positive spectral zero in Hz?
rectangle-first-zero.explain: X(f)∝sinc(fT), so the first positive zero is 1/T=50 Hz.

sampling-period.prompt: At a uniform sampling rate fs=1000 Hz, what is the sampling period in milliseconds?

dft-frequency-grid.prompt: At fs=800 Hz, 400 actual samples are collected without zero padding. What is the DFT bin spacing in Hz?
dft-frequency-grid.explain: Δf=fs/N=2 Hz; grid spacing is not a universal measure of actual resolvability.

real-spectrum-conjugate.prompt: A real periodic signal has F₂=2+j(3). What is the imaginary part of F₋₂?
real-spectrum-conjugate.explain: For a real signal F₋n=F_n*, which negates the imaginary part to -3.

periodic-transform-weight.prompt: A periodic signal has F₁=2. Its Fourier-transform impulse at ω=Ω has weight Kπ. Find K.

laplace-right-roc.prompt: For x=e^(−2t)u(t), the bilateral Laplace ROC is Re(s)>b. Find b.
laplace-right-roc.explain: Convergence requires Re(s+2)>0, so b=−2; the boundary is excluded.

laplace-left-roc.prompt: X(s)=1/(s+2) has ROC Re(s)<−2. What is its bilateral inverse?
laplace-left-roc.explain: A left-half-plane ROC selects a left-sided exponential with a negative sign.

unilateral-derivative-value.prompt: Using the unilateral Laplace transform from 0−, f(0−)=2 and F(1)=5. Find L[f′] at s=1.

laplace-initial-value.prompt: For causal F(s)=2/(s+3), with no impulse in f, find f(0+).

laplace-final-value.prompt: Causal F(s)=6/[s(s+2)] has all poles of sF strictly in the LHP. Find f(∞).

laplace-repeated-pole.prompt: For causal X(s)=6/(s+2)³ and x(t)=A t²e^(−2t)u(t), find A.

partial-fraction-residue.explain: Multiply by (s+1) and set s=−1: A=1/(2−1)=1.

inductor-initial-term.prompt: With passive reference directions, an inductor has L=2 H and i(0−)=3 A. In unilateral V=sLI+c, find c.

transfer-zero-location.prompt: For reduced H(s)=(s+3)/[(s+1)(s+2)], where is its finite zero?
transfer-zero-location.explain: The numerator vanishes at s=−3, with no common denominator factor.

transfer-rightmost-pole.prompt: For H(s)=1/[(s+1)(s+3)], what is the real part of its rightmost pole?
transfer-rightmost-pole.explain: The poles are −1 and −3; the larger real part is −1.

absolute-impulse-integral.explain: h is nonnegative, so its absolute integral is 1.5<∞; the system is BIBO stable.

amplitude-decibels.prompt: An amplitude gain is |H|=10. What is 20log10|H| in dB?
amplitude-decibels.explain: Use 20log10 for an amplitude ratio, giving 20 dB.

lowpass-cutoff-radians.prompt: For H(s)=2/(s+2), what is the −3 dB cutoff angular frequency in rad/s?
lowpass-cutoff-radians.explain: The gain falls to 1/√2 of its DC value at ω=2 rad/s, not 2 Hz.

mason-single-loop.prompt: A signal-flow graph has only one forward path P=6 and one touching loop L=-2. What is the transfer gain?

mason-two-loops.prompt: There are only two nontouching loops L₁=0.5, L₂=0.25. What is Mason’s determinant Δ?

direct-two-integrators.prompt: A strictly proper order-2 transfer function uses the standard continuous-time direct-form II realization. How many integrators are required?
direct-two-integrators.explain: Standard direct-form II uses a shared chain of 2 state integrators.

rc-pole-location.prompt: A first-order RC low-pass has τ=0.1 s. Where is its pole in s⁻¹?
rc-pole-location.explain: H=1/(1+τs), so the pole is s=−1/τ=-10 s⁻¹.

hidden-unstable-mode.prompt: An implementation has an internal e^(1t) mode cancelled in its reduced input-output transfer function. Does the reduced H(s) prove internal asymptotic stability?
hidden-unstable-mode.option2: No: a hidden unstable mode may remain
hidden-unstable-mode.option3: Yes whenever the input is zero
hidden-unstable-mode.explain: Algebraic cancellation describes input-output behavior; internal asymptotic stability still requires the full state matrix.

workbench.title: Signal workbench
workbench.rule: Order: reverse → scale → shift. Positive s shifts right; a>1 stretches time.
workbench.impulseNote: The narrow pulse approximates an impulse with finite width. Its area before transformation equals the amplitude parameter; scaling time also scales area.
workbench.approximation: Inputs are sampled on [−8, 8] s. Convolution uses Σ x[k]h[n−k]·Δt with a full [−16, 16] s output. Infinite-duration signals are treated as zero outside the input window. Finite sampling and narrow-pulse approximation introduce numerical error.
workbench.resolutionWarning: The pulse is very narrow or the oscillation is fast relative to the sampling grid. Increase the time scale or pulse width, or lower the frequency before comparing fine details.
